issues.legal_issue: A final determination of an issue by a court competent to decide that issue can bar its relitigation in a subsequent civil suit even when the earlier court could not have tried the subsequent suit, including where the claimant litigates under the title of a party to the earlier proceeding.
material_facts: Earlier civil suits, decided after the parties had an opportunity to contest the issues, determined that one alleged son had not been adopted by the property owner and that another person had been adopted by him.
The earlier determinations concerned issues raised again in the subsequent suit for possession.
The claimant was not personally a party to all the earlier proceedings, but claimed through a person who had been a party to them.
The court deciding the earlier proceedings was competent to decide the issues, although it could not have tried the subsequent suit.
issues.conclusion: The earlier determinations operated as res judicata against the claimant, who was litigating under the same title as the earlier party, and the issues could not be reopened in the subsequent suit.
issues.legal_principle: Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, including Explanation VIII, gives effect to final determinations by a court competent to decide the issue, notwithstanding that the court could not try the later suit. Res judicata promotes finality and prevents repeated litigation of the same issue. The Court relied on the general principles discussed in Gulabchand Chhotalal Parikh v. State of Gujarat and on Explanation VIII to Section 11.

rule.if: subsequent_civil_suit_reopens_same_issue and prior_issue_finally_decided_after_fair_hearing and prior_court_competent_to_decide_issue and (claimant_was_prior_party or claimant_claims_under_prior_party)

predicates.subsequent_civil_suit_reopens_same_issue: A party to a later civil suit raises an issue that was determined in an earlier proceeding.
predicates.prior_issue_finally_decided_after_fair_h: The earlier proceeding finally determined the issue after the affected parties had an opportunity to contest it.
predicates.prior_court_competent_to_decide_issue: The court in the earlier proceeding had authority to decide the issue, even if it could not have tried the later suit.
predicates.claimant_was_prior_party: The claimant in the later suit was a party to the earlier proceeding.
predicates.claimant_claims_under_prior_party: The claimant in the later suit claims through a person who was a party to the earlier proceeding.

issues.definition: When a later civil suit reopens an issue finally and fairly decided by a court competent to decide it, the issue cannot be relitigated if the claimant was, or claims under, a party to the earlier proceeding.

issues.legal_issue: A procedural amendment governing the effect of earlier issue determinations applies to a civil suit that was pending when the amendment took effect, absent an applicable exclusion.
material_facts: The suit in which the earlier determinations were invoked remained pending when the relevant amendment came into force.
The amendment concerned the procedural operation of prior decisions as res judicata.
The amending provisions did not exclude the amendment to the res judicata provision from the general rule governing pending proceedings.
issues.conclusion: The amended procedural provision applied to the pending suit.
issues.legal_principle: Section 97(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure Amendment Act, 1976 applies the amended Code to pending suits except where otherwise provided. Procedural provisions are generally presumed to apply to pending proceedings unless the text or necessary intendment indicates otherwise. The Court relied on Jose Da Costa v. Bascora Sadasiva Sinai Narcornim, as well as the principles in Delhi Cloth and General Mills Co. Ltd. v. Income Tax Commissioner, Garikapati Veeraya v. N. Subbiah Choudhary, Gurbachan Singh v. Satpal Singh, and the cited English authorities.

predicates.civil_suit_pending_when_procedural_chang: A civil suit remained pending when a legal change took effect.
predicates.change_concerns_procedure: The legal change concerns the procedure by which a court determines or gives effect to a matter.
predicates.no_exclusion_applies: No applicable provision or necessary implication excludes pending suits from the change.

issues.definition: A procedural change governs a civil suit that was pending when it took effect if no applicable exclusion prevents that result.

issues.legal_issue: A widow's adoption of a child to her deceased husband is not valid without the husband's authority under the applicable pre-statutory adoption law.
material_facts: A widow adopted a child decades after her husband had died, purporting to adopt the child to him.
The evidence established the fact of the adoption and the adoption ceremony, but did not establish express authority from the husband to adopt a son to him.
The claimant relied on the adoption to assert rights in the husband's family property.
issues.conclusion: The adoption to the deceased husband was not legally valid because no authority from him to make that adoption was proved.
issues.legal_principle: Section 8 of the Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act, 1956 addresses a widow's right to adopt a child for herself but is silent on adoption to her deceased husband. For the latter, the Court applied the Shastric law requiring the husband's express authority to the widow to adopt a child to him.

predicates.adoption_claim_is_to_deceased_husband: The adoption is asserted to have made the child a son of the widow's deceased husband.
predicates.widow_adopted_child_after_husband_died: A widow adopted a child after her husband had died.
predicates.no_authority_from_husband_was_proved: The evidence did not establish that the husband had authorized the widow to adopt a child to him.

issues.definition: An adoption made by a widow to her deceased husband is invalid when the husband had not authorized her to make it.

issues.legal_issue: A person adopted by a widow cannot use a legal fiction of being the son of the widow's deceased husband to claim an independent coparcenary right in that husband's property, and must claim, if entitled, through the widow.
material_facts: Earlier final decisions had rejected the asserted adoption of the widow's husband by the property owner.
The claimant was adopted by the widow long after the property owner's death and claimed rights in that property as the deceased husband's adopted son.
The claimant argued that adoption deemed him to have been born earlier and therefore gave him an independent right in the property.
The Court held that the claimant's entitlement, if any, was through the widow and not independently as a coparcener.
issues.conclusion: The claimant could not claim an independent right in the property as a deemed son or coparcener through the deceased husband; any claim had to be through the widow.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied clause (c) of the proviso to Section 12 of the Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act, 1956, under which an adopted child does not divest a person of an estate vested before the adoption. It rejected the proposed legal fiction of an earlier birth conferring an independent coparcenary claim, particularly where the deceased husband's adoption had already been rejected in prior proceedings.

predicates.adoption_based_property_claim: A person relies on an adoption to claim an interest in family property.
predicates.prior_decision_rejected_deceased_husband: A prior final decision rejected the asserted adoption of the widow's deceased husband into the property-owning family.
predicates.claimant_seeks_independent_coparcenary_r: The claimant asserts an independent coparcenary right based on being treated as the deceased husband's son.

issues.definition: If a property claim based on adoption follows a prior rejection of the deceased husband's adoption and asserts an independent coparcenary right, the claim must be made through the adoptive widow instead.
